title: Revisiting Self-Attention for Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation

problem.claim: Cross-domain sequential recommendation aims to predict future behaviors from user interactions across multiple domains.

gap.claim: Existing frameworks add domain-specific components but overlook the self-attention module's ability to learn correlations among behaviors.

contributions.claim: AutoCDSR formulates cross-domain learning as a multi-objective problem using Pareto-optimal self-attention to optimize recommendation while dynamically minimizing cross-domain attention scores.
AutoCDSR automates knowledge transfer by mitigating negative transfer and encouraging complementary knowledge exchange among auxiliary domains.
AutoCDSR+ extends the approach as a more performant variant with slight additional cost.

stated_novelty.claim: The work presents enhancing self-attention as a novel perspective for improving cross-domain sequential recommendation.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on large-scale production recommender data and academic benchmarks reportedly show consistent improvements over base transformers.
AutoCDSR reportedly enables simple models to perform on par with state-of-the-art methods with less overhead, including being 4x faster than state-of-the-art CDSR models.
On average, AutoCDSR raises Recall@10 for SASRec and Bert4Rec by 9.8% and 16.0%, respectively, and NDCG@10 by 12.0% and 16.7%, respectively.

narrative_sequence.summary: Sequential recommendation is established as a common recommender-systems paradigm, with cross-domain sequential recommendation identified as a challenging problem.
Existing CDSR methods rely on self-attention while adding domain-specific components, but the authors argue that these methods underuse the core self-attention module.
The work enhances self-attention through a Pareto-optimal, multi-objective formulation and introduces AutoCDSR for automated knowledge transfer.
AutoCDSR+ is introduced as a more performant variant, while the approach is described as plug-and-play and inexpensive to deploy.
Experiments on production and academic data report consistent gains, competitive performance, lower overhead, and improvements on Recall@10 and NDCG@10.

source_observation.claim: The approach improves cross-domain recommendation by modifying self-attention rather than adding separate domain-specific modules.

interpretation.claim: Core-model mechanisms may provide a simpler way to manage cross-domain transfer than extensive architectural additions.

application.claim: When adapting transformer recommenders across domains, consider multi-objective attention mechanisms that explicitly regulate cross-domain interactions.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether the reported benefits generalize beyond the evaluated production data and academic benchmarks.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify dataset sizes, domain composition, or experimental protocols.
The abstract does not provide baseline identities, statistical significance, or detailed computational-cost measurements.
The abstract does not describe the method's failure cases or sensitivity to hyperparameters.
